gloss_en: den and einen for a masculine direct object; die, das, eine and ein do not change

payload.explanation_en: The direct object of a verb stands in the accusative. Only the masculine article changes: der becomes den, ein becomes einen and kein becomes keinen. Feminine, neuter and plural articles are the same as in the nominative.
payload.pattern: der becomes den, ein becomes einen; die, das, eine stay the same

gloss_en: mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch, sie, Sie

payload.explanation_en: A personal pronoun that is the direct object stands in the accusative. ich becomes mich, du becomes dich and er becomes ihn. sie, es and Sie do not change.
payload.pattern: ich mich, du dich, er ihn, sie sie, es es, wir uns, ihr euch, sie sie, Sie Sie

examples.text: Das ist Herr Braun. Kennst du ihn?
examples.gloss_en: That is Mr Braun. Do you know him?

payload.explanation_en: es gibt says that something exists or is available. The form is the same for one thing and for many. The thing that exists stands in the accusative, so a masculine noun takes einen or keinen.

examples.text: In diesem Haus gibt es keinen Aufzug.
examples.gloss_en: There is no lift in this building.

gloss_en: not: makes a verb, an adjective or a whole sentence negative

payload.explanation_en: nicht makes a sentence negative. In a simple sentence it comes at the end. It comes before an adjective or adverb, before a phrase with a preposition, and before the verb part that stands at the end of the sentence.
payload.pattern: verb ... nicht; nicht + adjective; nicht + preposition phrase

examples.gloss_en: I do not live in Berlin.

gloss_en: no, not a, not any: makes a noun negative

payload.explanation_en: kein makes a noun negative when the positive sentence has ein or no article. It takes the same endings as ein. A noun with der, die, das or a possessive article is made negative with nicht.
payload.pattern: ein becomes kein, eine becomes keine, einen becomes keinen

examples.gloss_en: I do not have a car.
He does not have a brother.

gloss_en: mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, ihr, Ihr

payload.explanation_en: A possessive article says whose something is. Each person has its own word. The ending follows the noun as with ein: no ending before a der word or a das word, an e before a die word and before a plural.
payload.pattern: mein Bruder, meine Schwester, mein Kind, meine Eltern

examples.gloss_en: Our teacher is called Mrs Fischer.

gloss_en: meinen, deinen, seinen, ihren: en before a masculine direct object

payload.explanation_en: In the accusative only the masculine form changes, as with ein: mein becomes meinen. The feminine, neuter and plural forms are the same as in the nominative.
payload.pattern: meinen Bruder, meine Schwester, mein Kind, meine Eltern

lemma: modal verbs können, müssen, wollen, present tense
gloss_en: kann, muss, will: no ending with ich and er, a different vowel in the singular

payload.explanation_en: Modal verbs change their vowel in the singular and have no ending in the ich form and in the er, sie, es form. The plural is regular. können says what someone is able to do or what is possible, müssen says what is necessary, wollen says what someone wants.
payload.pattern: ich kann, du kannst, er kann, wir können, ihr könnt, sie können

examples.gloss_en: You have to go to the doctor.
He wants to work in Germany.

gloss_en: modal verb in second position, infinitive at the end

payload.explanation_en: In a sentence with a modal verb, the modal verb is conjugated and stands in second position. The other verb stays in the infinitive and goes to the very end of the sentence. Everything else stands between the two. In a yes or no question the modal verb comes first.
payload.pattern: modal verb in position two ... infinitive at the end

examples.gloss_en: I have to get up early tomorrow.

examples.text: Wir wollen am Samstag einen Ausflug machen.

gloss_en: the prefix goes to the end of the sentence: ich stehe auf

payload.explanation_en: Some verbs have a prefix that separates, such as an, auf, ein, fern and mit. In the present tense the verb is conjugated in second position and the prefix goes to the end of the sentence. After a modal verb the infinitive stays in one piece at the end. The prefixes be, er and ver never separate.

examples.text: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.

gloss_en: the past with haben and the participle at the end: ich habe gelernt

payload.explanation_en: The Perfekt is the usual way to talk about the past in spoken German. Most verbs build it with the present tense of haben in second position and the past participle at the end of the sentence.
payload.pattern: haben in position two ... participle at the end

gloss_en: the past with sein for verbs of movement: ich bin gefahren

payload.explanation_en: Verbs that say someone moves from one place to another build the Perfekt with sein instead of haben, for example gehen, fahren, kommen, fliegen and aufstehen. So do sein and bleiben. The participle stands at the end of the sentence.
payload.pattern: sein in position two ... participle at the end

gloss_en: ge and t for regular verbs, ge and en for many irregular verbs

payload.explanation_en: Regular verbs form the participle with ge, the stem and t: machen, gemacht. Many common irregular verbs end in en and often change the vowel: essen, gegessen. These are learned one by one. In a separable verb ge stands between the prefix and the stem: einkaufen, eingekauft. Verbs with the prefixes be, er and ver and verbs in ieren take no ge: besuchen, besucht.
payload.pattern: ge + stem + t; ge + stem + en

examples.gloss_en: We went shopping at the supermarket.
